blocks.markdown: **NEEDS VERIFICATION (D-01): syllabus citation vs statute.** The syllabus lists Section 121.2 under Trade Name, but the reviewer flags that provision as the collective-mark definition: “The syllabus cites 121.2 under Trade Name, but this is the statutory definition of collective mark. The actual trade-name definition is Section 121.3.” Both provisions are shown below and the error is not silently corrected — verify against the primary source (RA 8293) before reciting.

**Collective mark (Sec. 121.2 — the exact provision cited in the syllabus under Trade Name).** Any visible sign designated as such in the registration application and capable of distinguishing the origin or any other common characteristic — including quality — of the goods or services of different enterprises using the sign under the control of the registered owner.

**Trade name (Sec. 121.3 — the actual trade-name definition).** The name or designation identifying or distinguishing an enterprise. A trade name identifies the enterprise itself, not a particular product; a trademark identifies goods or services.

Origin or common characteristic of different enterprises' goods/services under the owner's control.

blocks.markdown: A name or designation may not be used as a trade name if, by its nature or use, it is contrary to public order or morals — particularly if liable to deceive trade circles or the public as to the nature of the enterprise it identifies. The prohibition focuses on public order/morals and deception about the enterprise's nature.

Trade names are protected even prior to or without registration against any unlawful third-party act, notwithstanding registration laws. Any subsequent use of the trade name — as a trade name, mark or collective mark — or of a similar name or mark likely to mislead the public is deemed unlawful. Sections 153–156 and 166–167 remedies apply mutatis mutandis. Ownership changes only with transfer of the enterprise or relevant part, with Sections 149.2–149.4 applying mutatis mutandis.

**Lyceum's limits.** Use the case for genericity and secondary meaning — a generic or descriptive class term is not exclusively appropriable absent proven secondary meaning — not as a direct modern Section 165 holding; the decision arose in the corporate-name context.
